job  ahead  involved  at  once  larger  shipment  to  countries  already  served  and
the  extension  of  aid  to  new  areas  of  acute  distress.
For  countries  already  served,  provision,  in  time,  of  immediate  continuing
needs—of  food,  clothing,  medicine,  shelter  and  transportation,  and  of  the
“necessary  supplies  (seeds,  fertilizers,  farm  tools  and  machinery)  for  spring
sowing,  was  a  primary  objective.  Only  so  could  some  degree  of  self-
sufficiency  in  food  be  secured  for  peoples  who,  beyond  1946,  in  Europe,
.  and  beyond  March  31,  1947,  in  the  Far  East,  could  count  on  no  further
help  from  UNRRA.  Shipments  of  over  50,000  tons  of  seed  were  being
speeded  for  delivery  to  9  European  countries  and  to  China.  By  the  fulfill
ment  of  minimum  requirements  now,  UNRRA  diminished  the  necessity
for  direct  relief  in  the  future.
Like  provision  of supplies  for  industrial  rehabilitation  could  alone  prevent
a  relapse—even  collapse—of  the  various  national  economies,  or  an  indefi-
nite  protraction  of  economic  crisis  and  stagnation.  ‘Some  measure  of  self-
sufficiency  was  paramount  if  all  UNRRA’s  work  was  not  to  be  undone.
Rehabilitation  remained  harnessed  and  subservient  to  relief.  Even  par-
tial  restoration  of  prewar  standards  lay  far  beyond  either  the  defined  scope
of  UNRRA'’s  work,  the  period  of  its  operations  or  the  means  at  its  disposal.
If  only  the  litter,  so  to  speak,  could  be  removed,  men  might  begin  to  tread
again  the  long  road  toward  recovery.  But  by  December  a  new  emergency
arose  which  affected  the  character  of forward  shipments  and  the  whole  plan
for  the  gradual  transfer  of  emphasis  from  emergency  relief  to  shipment  of
rehabilitation  goods.  :

29

[PDF page 30]
The  occasion  for  this  emergency  merits  brief  review.  In  mid-1945  it  was
estimated  that  wheat  supplies  would  be  ample  to  meet  the  needs  of  all
importing  countries.  But  by  August  the  picture  had  changed—for  the
worse.  As  the  result  of  disastrous  crop  failures  in  the  Mediterranean  basin,
receiving  countries  in  Europe  submitted  urgent  requests  for  increased  grain
shipments—for  Czechoslovakia  an  increase  of  200,000  tons,  for  Poland  a
forward  demand  ot  500,000  tons.  (Poland  normally  exports  surplus  grain.)
Moreover,  to  sustain  even  marginal  subsistence  in  urban  areas  throughout
Germany,  huge  increases  of wheat  supplies  were  needed.
Meanwhile  the  situation  was  further  aggravated  by  conditions  in  the
Far  East.  By  December,  rice  crops  were  known  to  be  gravely  disappointing.
With  rice  in  very  short  supply  (none  was  procurable  before  July  1945),
substantial  increase  of  wheat  shipments  to  China  became  paramount.
Eleventh  hour  advices,  further,  showed  need  for  importing  23  million  metric
tons  of rice  and/or  wheat  into Japan.
Thus  the  curve  of  demand  rose,  steeply  and  suddenly,  throughout  the
world.  These  enormous  additional  demands,  superimposed  on  crop  failures
in  Europe,  failure  of  the  Australian  crop  in  1944,  the  short  Argentine  crop
in  1944,  and  the  short  Canadian  crop  in  1945,  resulted  in  an  ugly  gap
between  import  requirements  and  available  supplies.
On  top  of  supply  shortages  came  shipping  and  transportation  shortages.
As,  on  oaqe  front,  the  situation  eased,  it  grew  worse  on  another.  Thus,  in
December,  shipments  of  all  sorts  from  the  United  States  were  seriously  cur-
tailed  by  lack  of  crews.  Grain  was  available.  Ships  were  not.  In  Jan-
uary,  when  ships  were  again  available,  transportation  troubles  prevented
grain  deliveries  to  dock  side.  Extreme  difficulties,  amounting  to  an  emer-
gency,  had  developed  in  moving  available  grain  from  the  producing  areas
throughout  the  world  to  ports  of  shipment.  At  the  close  of  the  year  there
was  in  sight  an  insufficiency  of  grain  to  meet  UNRRA’s  scheduled  re-
quirements  for  the  critical  month  of January  1946.  :
Thus,  at  the  close  of  1945,  instead  of  ample  provision  for  all,  a  wheat
deficit  was  indicated  of  195  million  bushels  (or  5%  million  long  tons)  for  the
period  ending June  1946.  The  incidence  of  crisis  would  be  greatest  between
January  and  June  1946.  The  requirements  of  invaded  countries  for  this
period  exceeded  the  supply  available  by  42  percent.
Shortage  of  fats  and  oils  were  even  worse,  but  here  the  trouble  was ss  of  long
standing.  During  the  second  half  of  1945,  UNRRA  was  able  to  ship  less
than  20  percent  of  the  requirements  in  countries  desperately  in  need.  For-
ward  prospects  suggested  small  improvement.
Thus  UNRRA’s  provision  for  emergency  relief,  to  avert  death  and  starva-
tion,  continued  a  first  charge  on  its  operations.  The  gradual  transfer  of
emphasis  to  provision  of  agricultural  and  industrial  rehabilitation  supplies
had  to  be  deferred.  UNRRA  coatinued  locked  in  a  struggle  to  secure  sur-
vival.  It  is  against  such  facts  and  figures  that  the  achievements  of  a  record
quarter  must  be  read.  For  they  provide  an  index,  not  only  of  the  limits  of

30

[PDF page 31]
UNRRA’s  capacity  to  help,  but  of  the  slow,  precarious  pace  of  world
recovery.
But,  beyond  countries  already  in  receipt  of  substantial  aid,  UNRRA
faced  new  extended  liabilities.  Concurrently  with  the  procurement  and
shipment  of  relief  supplies,  planning  proceeded  rapidly  for  new  and  exact-
ing  relief  and  rehabilitation  operations.

Byelorussian  and  Ukrainian  Soviet  Republics
Two  Soviet  Republics,  Byelorussia  and  the  Ukraine,  had  qualified  for
relief  assistance.  In  these  two  republics  the  destruction  of  war  had  reached
a  scale  never  before  known  in  history.  Twice  their  territories  were  a  battle-
ground—once  when  the  tide  of invasion  reached  to  Moscow  and  Stalingrad,
and  again  when  the  enemy  was  driven  out  by  the  victorious  Russian  armies.
The  enemy  removed  virtually  all  agricultural  machinery.  Livestock  was
decimated.  All  movable  stocks  of  food,  and  even  of  seeds,  were  removed.
City  after  city  was  totally  destroyed.  More  than  25,000,000  were  left
with  homes  completely  wrecked.
Forward  provision  was  made  during  the  quarter  for  relief  programs
amounting  to  $189  million  for  the  Ukraine  and  $61  million  for  Byelorussia.
First  shipments  began  before  the  end  of  the  year  (6  vessels  sailing  in  Novem-
ber,  7  in  December)  carrying  food  and  medical  supplies.  Formal  agree-
ments,  substantially  the  same  as  those  made  with  other  countries,  were
signed  on  December  18.  Under  these  agreements  the  two  Soviet  Republics
will  grant  to  UNRRA'’s  missions  privileges  and  immunities  similar  to
those  granted  to foreign  governments.  These  include  inviolability  of  the
mission’s  archives  and  premises,  exemption  from  taxes  and  immunity  from
suit  and  legal  process  with  regard  to  activities  exercised  within  the  scope
of  their  authority  under  the  agreement.  They  provide  also  for  complete
freedom  for  UNRRA  officials  to  observe  the  equitable  distribution  of
supplies  which  UNRRA  delivers.

Austria
The  extension  of  relief  operations  to  Austria  was  authorized  by  action
of  the  Council.  Late  in  the  quarter  a  formal  request,  by  the  Allied  Control
Council,  was  received  for  immediate  relief.  Conditions  in  the  country
are  desperate.  By  December  it  was  estimated  that  10,000  would  be  dying  °
of  tuberculosis  in  Vienna  alone.  UNRRA,  it  is  feared,  will  only  be  able
to  undertake  part  of  the  relief  needed  to  avert  a  tragedy.

ltaly
The  occasion  for  extended  relief  to  Italy  has  been  previously  outlined.
During  the  quarter,  plans  were  laid  and  a  draft  agreement  negotiated
with  the  Italian  Government  for  the  expansion  of  UNRRA’s  work  in  1946

to  cover  a  program  to  cost  between  $400-$500  millions.  Large  as  the

tinuance  of  imports  of  essential  civilian  supplies  provided,  until  August
1945,  by  the  military  authorities  under  their  formula  for  “prevention  of
disease  and  of  unrest.”  Not  more  than  half  of  Italy’s  urgently  needed  im-

chaos.  More  help  than  it  can  give  is  needed  before  Italy  can  stand  on
its  own  feet  again—and  not  stagger  for  the  weakness  in  it.

Relief  to  Korea  and  Formosa  was  authorized  by  the  Council  in  August

operation,  planning  and  procurement  had  reached  an  advanced  stage
before  the  end  of  1945.  :  :

PRESIDENT'S  LETTER  OF  TRANSMITTAL

To  THE  CONGRESS  OF  THE  UNITED  STATES  OF  AMERICA:

I  am  transmitting  herewith  the  sixth  report  to  Congress  on  UNRRA
operations  for  the  quarter  ending  December  31,  1945.
During  this  quarter,  while  UNRRA’s  shipments  reached  unprecedented
figures,  recipient  countries  experienced  unprecedented  needs.  Crop  failures
resulted  in  the  continuance  of  near  famine  conditions.  The  hardships  of
winter  were  imminent.
At  year’s  end,  moreover,  critical  shortages  (notably  of  wheat,  fats,  meat
for  Europe,  and  of  rice  for  China)  threatened  execution  of  even  the  limited
relief  program  that  had  been  planned.  For  millions  survival  was,  and  still
is,  the  issue,  and  for  UNRRA  the  challenge  to  be  met.  World  recovery
still  remains  a  formidable  task.
Only  concerted  action  by  the  United  Nations  (and,  primarily,  of  the
producing  countries)  can,  even  at  this  date,  avert  the  prolongation  of
emergency  conditions  throughout  the  world.  Now,  more  than  ever,  inten-
sified  efforts  to  match  need  with  supply,  are  required  of  us.  We  must  not
fail.  For  our  continued  participation  in  UNRRA  marks  the  fulfillment  of
a  pledge  and  the  discharge  of  a  debt  to  those  who,  beyond  the  common
sacrifice  of  life  and  material  resources,  endured  the  devastation  and  bru-
talities  that  we  were  spared.  Conscience  alone  demands  that  we  meet  the
full  measure  of  our  obligation.
But  prudence  and  self-interest  no  less  dictate  our  policy.  Neither  peace
nor  prosperity  can  be  assured  to  us  while  famine,  disease  and  destitution
deprive  others  of  the  means  to  live,  let  alone  to  prosper.  Relief and  rehabil-
itation  are  paramount  necessities  for  that  world  recovery  which  is  a  primary
objective  of  our  national  policy.  They  provide  the  best  insurance  against
social  chaos  and  moral  disintegration  and  the  surest  guarantee  for  the
growth  of  democratic  modes  of  thought  and  action.  The  emergency,
which  UNRRA  was  designed  to  meet,  continues.  The  months  immedi-
ately  ahead  are  critical.
While  ours  is  the  largest  contribution  to  UNRRA’s  funds,  it  is  matched
by  like,  proportionate  contributions  of  30  other  nations.  This  gives  sig-
nificance  to  UNRRA  altogether  beyord  the  relief  that  it  provides.  In
UNRRA  the  United  Nations  have  created  the  first  international  operating
agency  through  which  to  test  and  to  perfect  our  powers  of  cooperation.
Such  powers  are  not  inborn.  They  are  cultivated,  by  constant  exercise
and  the  progressive  enlargement  of  mutual  experience.  In  UNRRA  a
precedent  has  been  created  that  may  prove  a  landmark  in  our  progress
toward  solidarity  and  common  action  by  the  nations  of  the  world.

Chapter  1
WAR'S  AFTERMATH
The  “cease  fire”  order  which,  for  most  Americans,  signalled  the  resump-
tion  of  peacetime  pursuits,  carried  a  sterner  message  to  the  people  of Europe
and  the  Far  East.  For  them  it  meant  the  redepleyment  of  their  moral  and
material  resources  against  new  enemies.  War  did  not  so  much  end  as
change  front.  Men  entered  on  a  struggle  with  conditions  described  300
years  ago:
“In  such  condition  there  is  no  place  for  industry,  because  the  fruit  thereof
is  uncertain,  and  consequently,  no  culture  of  the  earth,  no  navigation,  nor
use  of  the  commodities  that  may  be  imported  by  sea,  no  commodious  build-
ing,  no  instruments  of  moving  and  removing  such  things  as  require  much
force;  and  which  is  worst  of  all,  continual  fear  and  danger  of death;  and  the
life  of  man  solitary,  poor,  nasty,  brutish  and  short.”
The  summer  months,  preceding  the  period  here  under  review,  brought,
it  is  true,  brief  respite  of  clement  weather.  But  they  brought  little  else  of
comfort.  As,  throughout  1945,  men  and  women  strove  to  repair  the
damages  of  war,  the  full  significance  of  the  break-down  of  all  the  sinews  of
organized  society  became  increasingly  apparent.  :
Starvation,  plague,  exposure,  isolation—these  and  other  ills  could  have
been  dealt  with  singly.  But  collectively  they  made  for  liabilities  in  which
the  total  was  more  than  the  sum  of  all  the  parts.  Their  needs  and  their
distresses  inter-acted,  one  aggravating  another  and  increasing  their  over-all
predicament.

Manpower  Short
In  and  out  of  government,  manpower  was  short.  In  Yugoslavia,  every
seventh  person  had  been  killed,  in  Greece,  one  man  in  8,  in  Poland,  one
in  6.  The  training,  too,  of  skilled  personnel  had  come  to  a  virtual  stand-
still  during  the  war  years.
Equipment  Destroyed
In  industry  and  on  the  farm,  loss  of  equipment  aggravated  the  man-
power  shortage.  In  Czechoslovakia,  25,000  citizens  responded  to  a  call
to  man  the  mines.  Bankers  and  clerks,  doctors  and  lawyers,  hauled  out
the  coal  with  hand  and  shovel.  In  Yugoslavia,  absence  of  ploughs  and

field,  singlehanded,  with  an  axe.  2,

No  Trucks,  No  Trains
In  the  Silesian  mines,  machinery  was  intact,  but  here,  as  elsewhere,
another  ill  assailed  them.  Freight  cars  and  trucks  were  lacking.  Coal  at
the  pithead  stood  for  sale  at  360  zlotys.  In  faraway  Warsaw  it  fetched
8,000  zlotys.  Wheat,  harvested  by  hand  with  superhuman  effort,  lay
rotting  for  lack  of  transport  to  carry  it  to  areas  where  people  starved.

No  Food,  No  Clothes,  No  Shelter
Lack  of  shelter,  of  food  and  clothing  likewise  added  to  cumulative  strains,
taking  their  toll  in  sickness,  debility  and  death.  In  Yugoslavia,  one-half  a
million  homes  were  destroyed  (one  Bosnian  village,  during  the  war,  had
changed  hands  56  times).  In  Italy  400,000  people  were  without  shelter;
in  Warsaw  men  and  boys  searched  the  rubble  of  the  ruins  for  scraps  of
roofing  paper  with  which  to  cover  their  feet;  in  Greece,  more  than  half  the
population  were  still  without  minimum  clothing  needs..  From  Doboj,  in
Yugoslavia,  the  Germans  had  removed  even  swaddling  clothes,  as  padding
for  their  tanks.  Towns  and  villages  all  across  Europe  told  the  same  story,
“Nema  mishta”—there  is  nothing.

The  Crops  Fail
And,  as  though  war  and  its  aftermath  were  not  enough,  nature  conspired
to  thwart  men’s  first  painful  efforts  at  recovery.  Country  after  country  in
the  Mediterranean  basin  experienced  the  worst  drought  in  decades.  Har-
vests  fell  short  of  prewar  levels  by  50-60-70  percent.  Shortage  piled  on
shortage.  Prices  sky-rocketed  and  bewildered  men  and  women  fingered
money  that  had  lost  its  value.
Winter  Ahead
Conditions  such  as  these  persisted  into  late  summer  and  fall.  Some
became  aggravated.  And  ahead  was  winter.  The  first  frosts  came.
Villagers  in  Yugoslavia  kept  indoors  for  lack  of  footwear,  or  borrowed
from  a  neighbor.  Hospitals  had  no  heat.  In  Poland,  in  November,  a
train  steamed  in,  bringing  1,500  people  from  the  eastern  provinces.  They
had  travelled  in  open  cars  at  12  degrees  below  zero.  Six  children  froze
to  death.  In  Greece  mountain  villages  faced  the  prospect  of  complete
isolation  from  the  world  until  the  spring.  Everywhere  men  remained
preoccupied  with  bare  survival.  Recovery  was  a  mere  dream,  a  hope
deferred.
China's  Plight
‘As  in  the  west,  so  in  the  east.  In  Hankow,  the  Chinese  Chicago,  power
companies  and  factories  are  deathly  still.  Hands,  once  raised  to  cheer

Rural  Hunan  lies  fallow  this  year,  farms  and  villages  stripped  by  the
Japanese,  even  the  peasant’s  hand  tools  used  for  firewood.  The  rice  dykes
are  destroyed.  The  cracked  earth  will  yield  no  crops.
In  Tientsin  the  woolen  mills  are  idle.  Carts  in  Canton  still  make  their
grisly  rounds,  picking  the  corpses  off  the  streets.  The  railroad  station  in
Shanghai  is  now  wasteland.
And  everywhere,  from  Manchuria  to  the  southern  provinces,  new  armies
are  on  the  move—civilian  armies.  Refugees,  driven  three,  four,  five  times
over,  always  further  from  their  homes  by  the  invading  enemy,  and  now
making  the  great  trek  home,  penniless,  ragged,  feet  gangrenous,  inscrutable
in  their  sorrows,  inexplicably  full  of  hope.  Their  numbers  are  not  accu-
rately  known,  but  are  estimated  at  30-40  million.  Their  plight  is  beyond
description.
Such  is  the  partial  story  of  the  world’s  predicament.  =  No  record  in  history
survives  of  ruin  and  distress  so  universal.  F igures  that  seem  astronomical
(of  tonnages  and  dollar  values  of  relief  supplied)  dwindle  to  insignificance
beside  the  desolation  and  the  need.  These,  like  the  record  which  follows,
represent  only  the  first,  partial  contribution  made,  through  UNRRA,  by
the  United  Nations  to  salvage  life  and  restore  human  dignity  to  millions
still  in  the  throes  of  the  aftermath  of  war.

Chapter  2
ACHIEVEMENTS  OF  THE  QUARTER!

Before  April  1945  UNRRA'’s  activities  were  mainly  limited  to  the  advance
procurement  of  supplies  and  the  assembling  and  training  of  its  staff.  Ship-
ments  were  negligible.  Even  in  the  first  6  months  of  its operations  in  the
field  (from  April  to  September),  little  more  than  palliative  measures  had
proved  possible.  Relief  goods  were,  in  large  measure,  still  in  short  supply.
Shipping  remained  heavily  committed  to  military  needs.  As  the  fall  came,
time  pressed.  Hungry  and  homeless,  ill-clad,  ill-shod,  and  destitute—
millions  looked  with  dread  toward  winter’s  approach.  The  peak  of  crisis
soared  immediately  ahead.
It  was  to  this  emergency  that UNRRA  addressed  itself  in  the  last  quarter
of  1945.  With  supplies  and  shipping  now,  at  last,  more  readily  available,
the  relief  program  began  to  hit  its  stride.

Shipments  Increase

UNRRA  shipments  in  October  were  estimated  at  566,300  gross  long
tons,  a  record,  to  date.  458,600  tons  were  moved  from  the  Western
Hemisphere  alone,  the  bulk  of them  from  the  United  States.  In  November,
a  fresh  record  was  achieved.  Shipments  exceeded  those  even  of October  by
20  percent,  amounting  to  an  estimated  689,500  gross  long  tons.  523,080
tons  moved  out  of  ports  in  the  Western  Hemisphere,  the  bulk  of  them  from
the  United  States.  .
Owing,  chiefly,  to  shortage  of  ships  crews  in  the  United  States,  December
shipments  which,  it  had  been  hoped,  would  top  the  million  mark,  fell
short  of  expectations.  562,100  tons  were  shipped,  bringing  the  cumulative
total  for  the  year  to  3,959,300  tons.  The  last  quarter  of  the  year  ranked
first  in  the  volume  and  the  scale  of  the  relief provided,  though  this  continued
far  short  of  requirements  in  regard  to  some  essential  commodities.  World

The  main  objectives  of  the  quarter  were  two-fold—relief  from  the  ex-
tremes  of  present  need,  and  provision  for  the  future,  means  for  the  repair
of  industries  contributing  directly  to  relief  needs  and  for  the  recovery  of
agriculture  and  the  consequent  curtailment  of UNRRA’s  forward  liabilities.
The  more  and  the  quicker  men  helped  themselves,  the  less  and  the  shorter
the  need  for  external  assistance.
From  the  Western  Hemisphere,  food,  the  dominant,  immediate  need,
outstripped  by  far  all  other  shipments—in  October,  363,500  tons,  in Novem-

for  the  achievement  of  self-help  by  people  shorn  of  almost  everything  but

but  for  the  morrow—safest  insurance  against  the  unending  continuance  of

Gains  of  the  Quarter  Deferred

The  gains  of  the  quarter  were,  nevertheless,  decisive.  Millions  live  who,
but  for  UNRRA,  would  have  died.  The  suffering  of  further  millions  was
mitigated  by  the  provision  of  food  and  clothing,  shelter,  and  medicine.
The  importance,  moreover,  of what  has  been  averted  is  as  great  as  that  of
what  has  been  achieved.  Little  remarked,  but  of  high  significance,  is  the
total  absence  throughout  Europe  of any widespread  epidemics.  The  contrast
with  the  situation  at  the  end  of  World  War  I,  1914-1918,  is  striking.  Condi-
tions, widely  prevalent  in  almost  every  country,  were  an  open  invitation  to  in-
fection  and  the  spread  of disease.  Again  and  again,  UNRRA’s  medical  staff
~  has  helped  to  scotch  it  at  its  inception,  where  necessary,  flying  supplies  of
antitoxin,  DDT,  etc.,  by  plane  to  the  point  of  danger.  UNRRA  has
organized  the  largest  international  medical  relief  operation  in  history.  In
November  1945  there  were  800  UNRRA  physicians  and  nurses  at  work
in  Europe.
Pure  gain,  too,  has  been  the  steadily  increasing  delivery  of  rehabilitation
supplies.  While  these  have  not  always  shown  immediate  results,  they  will
earn  rich  dividends  as,  in  succeeding  months,  native  industries  increase
their  output  of basic  essential  supplies  and  the volume  of internal  trade  and  of
employment  increases,  thus  progressively  curtailing  UNRRA’s  burden  of
providing  help  from  outside  sources.  Already  countries  like  Poland  and
Czechoslovakia  have  produced  surpluses  which  they  have  made  available
for  the  relief  of  suffering  in  other  European  countries.  While  still  excep-
tional,  this  reciprocity  suggests  a  hopeful  trend.  Rewarding  dividends  will
likewise  be  paid  as,  in  springtime,  farmers  avail  themselves  of  tools  and  of
equipment  shipped  earlier  to  secure  spring  sowing.

Victims  of  a  peculiarly  tragic  fate  are  the  so-called  displaced  persons  of

children  were  torn  from  their  homes  and  scattered  like  chaff  across  three
continents,  either  as  refugees  or  as  impressed  slave  laborers  of  the  Axis
powers.  In  the  three  western  zones  of  occupied  Germany  alone,  they
numbered  over  6  million.  Hundreds  of  thousands  were  found  in  Italy
and  Austria,  thousands  more  in  Albania,  Greece,  the  Dodecanese  Islands,
Egypt,  Palestine,  Cyprus,  Ethiopia,  the  Belgian  Congo,  Tanganyika,  in
China,  and  the  Philippines.  In  enemy  territory,  once  their  usefulness  as
slave  laborers  ceased,  they  were  left  to  fend  for  themselves.  Many  were
starving,  ill-clothed  and  sick.  All  were  deprived  of  help  from  friends  and
neighbors  or  of  their  own  governments,  for  they  were  far  from  home.

The  occasion  for  this  emergency  merits  brief  review.  In  mid-1945  it  was
estimated  that  wheat  supplies  would  be  ample  to  meet  the  needs  of  all
importing  countries.  But  by  August  the  picture  had  changed—for  the
worse.  As  the  result  of  disastrous  crop  failures  in  the  Mediterranean  basin,
receiving  countries  in  Europe  submitted  urgent  requests  for  increased  grain
shipments—for  Czechoslovakia  an  increase  of  200,000  tons,  for  Poland  a
forward  demand  ot  500,000  tons.  (Poland  normally  exports  surplus  grain.)
Moreover,  to  sustain  even  marginal  subsistence  in  urban  areas  throughout
Germany,  huge  increases  of wheat  supplies  were  needed.
Meanwhile  the  situation  was  further  aggravated  by  conditions  in  the
Far  East.  By  December,  rice  crops  were  known  to  be  gravely  disappointing.
With  rice  in  very  short  supply  (none  was  procurable  before  July  1945),
substantial  increase  of  wheat  shipments  to  China  became  paramount.
Eleventh  hour  advices,  further,  showed  need  for  importing  23  million  metric
tons  of rice  and/or  wheat  into Japan.
Thus  the  curve  of  demand  rose,  steeply  and  suddenly,  throughout  the
world.  These  enormous  additional  demands,  superimposed  on  crop  failures
in  Europe,  failure  of  the  Australian  crop  in  1944,  the  short  Argentine  crop

between  import  requirements  and  available  supplies.
On  top  of  supply  shortages  came  shipping  and  transportation  shortages.

USSVI Creed
Section 1: To perpetuate the memory of our shipmates who gave their lives in the pursuit of their duties while

Perpetual Remembrance

of those shipmates who have given the supreme sacrifice. USSVI also endeavors to educate all third parties it
comes in contact with about the services United States submariners performed and how the sacrifices of lost

SILENT RUNNING
DECEMBER LOST BOATS
“I can assure you that they went down fighting and that their brothers who survived them took a
grim toll of our savage enemy to avenge their deaths."  Vice Admiral Charles A. Lockwood, USN

USS Capelin (SS-289)
Lost on Dec 2, 1943 with the loss of 76 men. She was on her 1st war patrol, but her exact location and
cause of loss remain a mystery. She may have been lost to mines or an operational casualty.

USS Sealion (SS-195)
Lost on Dec 10, 1941 with the loss of 5 men. To prevent her from falling into enemy hands, she was
scuttled in Manila Bay after incurring severe bomb damage during the initial Japanese attack. The de-
struction of the Navy Yard made repairs impossible, and Sealion was ordered destroyed. All salvagable
equipment was taken off, depth charges were placed inside, and the explosives were set off to prevent
her from being made useful to the enemy.

USS F1 / Carp (SS-20)
Lost on December 17, 1917 with the loss of 19 officers and men when it was sunk after collision with the
USS F-3 (Pickerel) (SS-22) off San Clemente, CA. While maneuvering in exercises at sea, F-1 and F-3
collided, the former sinking in 10 seconds, her port side torn forward of the engine room. 19 of her men
were lost, while 3 others were rescued by the submarines with whom she was operating.

USS S-4 (SS-109)
Lost on December 17, 1927 with the loss of 40 officers and men when it was sunk after being rammed
by USCG Paulding. Salvaged in 1928 and re-commissioned.

the new with the old. Although untried in combat, she was
one of the newest boats in the Submarine Service and in-
corporated the latest improvements in submarine design
and equipment. Moreover her "gallantly battle  -tested" crew
epitomized the "valor, skill, and dedicated service of sub-
mariners" during the long Pacific war. Thus, on her deck
that morning Fleet Admiral Nimitz read his orders assigning
him to duty as Chief of Naval Operations, and his relief,
Adm. Raymond A. Spruance, read orders making him
CINCPAC and CINPOA.

I liked sailors from all parts of the land, we trusted and de-  ============================================
pended on each other for competence, comradeship,
strength and courage. They were "shipmates"; then and
forever.
I liked the surge of adventure in my heart, when the word
was passed: "Now set the special sea and anchor detail -
all hands to quarters for leaving port," and I liked the thrill of
sighting home again, with the waving hands of welcome
from family and friends waiting pier side.
The work was hard and dangerous; the going rough at
times; the parting from loved ones painful, but the compan-
ionship of robust Navy laughter, the "all for one and one for
all" philosophy of the sea was ever present.
I liked the serenity of the sea after a day of hard ship's work, as  ============================================
flying fish flitted across the wave tops and sunset gave way
to night.
I liked the feel of the Navy in darkness -- the masthead and
range lights, the red and green navigation lights and stern
light, the pulsating phosphorescence of radar repeaters -
they cut through the dusk and joined with the mirror of stars
overhead. And I liked drifting off to sleep lulled by the myri-
ad of noises that told me that my ship was well, and that
my shipmates on watch would keep me safe.
I liked quiet midwatches with the aroma of strong coffee;
the lifeblood of the Navy permeating everywhere. And I
liked hectic watches when the exacting minuet of haze-gray
shapes racing at flank speed kept all hands on a razor
edge of alertness.  ============================================
I liked the sudden cry of "General quarters, general quar-
ters, all hands man your battle stations," followed by the
clamor of running feet on ladders and the resounding
thump of watertight doors as the ship transformed herself in
a few brief seconds from a peaceful workplace to a weapon
of war…ready for anything.
And I liked the sight of space-age equipment manned by
youngsters clad in dungarees and sound-powered phones
that their grandfathers would still recognize.
I liked the traditions of the Navy and those who made them.
I liked the proud names of Navy heroes: Halsey, Nimitz,  ============================================
Perry, Farragut, John Paul Jones and Burke. A sailor could
find much in the Navy: comrades-in-arms, pride in self and
country, mastery of the seaman's trade.
In years to come, when sailors are home from the sea, they
will still remember with fondness and respect the ocean in
all its moods - the impossible shimmering mirror calm or
the storm-tossed green water surging over the bow. And
then there will come again a faint whiff of stack gas, a faint
echo of engine and rudder orders, a vision of the bright  ============================================
bunting of signal flags snapping at the yardarm, a refrain of
hearty laughter in the wardroom and chief's quarters and
mess decks.
Gone ashore for good they will grow wistful about their Na-
vy days, when the seas belonged to them and a new port
of call was ever over the horizon.
Remembering this, they will stand taller and they will say, "I
WAS A SAILOR ONCE AND I WOULD DO IT AGAIN."
Writing by VADM. Harold Koenig, U.S.N. Ret.

USSVI Creed
Section 1: To perpetuate the memory of our shipmates who gave their lives in the pursuit of their duties while
serving their country that their dedication, deeds, and supreme sacrifice may be a constant source of motiva-
tion toward greater accomplishments, and to pledge loyalty and patriotism to the United States of America
and its Constitution.
Camaraderie
Section 2: In addition to perpetuating the memory of departed shipmates, USSVI shall provide a way for all
Submariners to gather for our mutual benefit and enjoyment. Our common heritage as Submariners shall be
strengthened by camaraderie. The USSVI supports a strong U.S. Submarine Force.
Perpetual Remembrance
Section 3: The organization engages in various projects and deeds that bring about the perpetual remembrance
of those shipmates who have given the supreme sacrifice. USSVI also endeavors to educate all third parties it
comes in contact with about the services United States submariners performed and how the sacrifices of lost
shipmates made possible the freedom and lifestyle American enjoy today

SILENT RUNNING
DECEMBER LOST BOATS
“I can assure you that they went down fighting and that their brothers who survived them took a
grim toll of our savage enemy to avenge their deaths."  Vice Admiral Charles A. Lockwood, USN

USS Capelin (SS-289)
Lost on Dec 2, 1943 with the loss of 76 men. She was on her 1st war patrol, but her exact location and
cause of loss remain a mystery. She may have been lost to mines or an operational casualty.

USS Sealion (SS-195)
Lost on Dec 10, 1941 with the loss of 5 men. To prevent her from falling into enemy hands, she was
scuttled in Manila Bay after incurring severe bomb damage during the initial Japanese attack. The de-
struction of the Navy Yard made repairs impossible, and Sealion was ordered destroyed. All salvagable
equipment was taken off, depth charges were placed inside, and the explosives were set off to prevent
her from being made useful to the enemy.

USS F1 / Carp (SS-20)
Lost on December 17, 1917 with the loss of 19 officers and men when it was sunk after collision with the
USS F-3 (Pickerel) (SS-22) off San Clemente, CA. While maneuvering in exercises at sea, F-1 and F-3
collided, the former sinking in 10 seconds, her port side torn forward of the engine room. 19 of her men
were lost, while 3 others were rescued by the submarines with whom she was operating.

USS S-4 (SS-109)
Lost on December 17, 1927 with the loss of 40 officers and men when it was sunk after being rammed
by USCG Paulding. Salvaged in 1928 and re-commissioned.

I liked sailors from all parts of the land, we trusted and de-  ============================================
pended on each other for competence, comradeship,
strength and courage. They were "shipmates"; then and
forever.
I liked the surge of adventure in my heart, when the word
was passed: "Now set the special sea and anchor detail -
all hands to quarters for leaving port," and I liked the thrill of
sighting home again, with the waving hands of welcome
from family and friends waiting pier side.
The work was hard and dangerous; the going rough at
times; the parting from loved ones painful, but the compan-
ionship of robust Navy laughter, the "all for one and one for
all" philosophy of the sea was ever present.
I liked the serenity of the sea after a day of hard ship's work, as  ============================================
flying fish flitted across the wave tops and sunset gave way
to night.
I liked the feel of the Navy in darkness -- the masthead and
range lights, the red and green navigation lights and stern
light, the pulsating phosphorescence of radar repeaters -
they cut through the dusk and joined with the mirror of stars
overhead. And I liked drifting off to sleep lulled by the myri-
ad of noises that told me that my ship was well, and that
my shipmates on watch would keep me safe.
I liked quiet midwatches with the aroma of strong coffee;
the lifeblood of the Navy permeating everywhere. And I
liked hectic watches when the exacting minuet of haze-gray
shapes racing at flank speed kept all hands on a razor
edge of alertness.  ============================================
I liked the sudden cry of "General quarters, general quar-
ters, all hands man your battle stations," followed by the
clamor of running feet on ladders and the resounding
thump of watertight doors as the ship transformed herself in
a few brief seconds from a peaceful workplace to a weapon
of war…ready for anything.
And I liked the sight of space-age equipment manned by
youngsters clad in dungarees and sound-powered phones
that their grandfathers would still recognize.
I liked the traditions of the Navy and those who made them.
I liked the proud names of Navy heroes: Halsey, Nimitz,  ============================================
Perry, Farragut, John Paul Jones and Burke. A sailor could
find much in the Navy: comrades-in-arms, pride in self and
country, mastery of the seaman's trade.
In years to come, when sailors are home from the sea, they
will still remember with fondness and respect the ocean in
all its moods - the impossible shimmering mirror calm or
the storm-tossed green water surging over the bow. And
then there will come again a faint whiff of stack gas, a faint
echo of engine and rudder orders, a vision of the bright  ============================================
bunting of signal flags snapping at the yardarm, a refrain of
hearty laughter in the wardroom and chief's quarters and
mess decks.
Gone ashore for good they will grow wistful about their Na-
vy days, when the seas belonged to them and a new port
of call was ever over the horizon.
Remembering this, they will stand taller and they will say, "I
WAS A SAILOR ONCE AND I WOULD DO IT AGAIN."

# 17.05.2023 The South Tyrolean Settlement in Reutte – A Piece of History in the Heart of the Town

Today, I would like to introduce you to a part of Reutte that you may not have discovered yet, even though it is located almost right in the town center and is well worth a visit – the South Tyrolean Settlement.

**Historical Background**

After the First World War, South Tyrol was officially awarded to Italy in the Treaty of Saint-Germain in 1919. Everyday life for the South Tyrolean population – around 90% of whom were German-speaking – became increasingly difficult. German-language schools were closed, and Italians from southern regions were resettled in the area. Following Austria’s annexation by Germany in March 1938, many South Tyroleans hoped that the new ruler, Adolf Hitler, would bring South Tyrol “back home to the Reich.” These hopes were dashed when the so-called “Option” was agreed upon in the Hitler–Mussolini Agreement.

**A Forced Choice**

The “Option” forced the German-speaking South Tyrolean population to make a dramatic decision:

– They could remain in South Tyrol, renounce their cultural identity, accept Italian citizenship, and still face the risk of being resettled elsewhere within Italy

or

– They could choose German citizenship, but would then be required to leave their homeland of South Tyrol and start a new life within the German Reich.

The bitter truth for everyone involved was that, regardless of their decision, they would lose their homeland of South Tyrol.

This so-called “choice” caused a deep and lasting division within society. Entire villages and families were torn apart – those who chose to stay (“Dableiber”) could not understand those who opted to leave (“Optanten”), and vice versa.

In the vote, around 80 percent – approximately 166,000 South Tyroleans – chose the option of adopting German citizenship and emigrating. By the end of the war, about 75,000 of them had actually left. Due to the outbreak of the Second World War, the resettlement process slowed down significantly and was eventually brought to a complete halt.

[![Image 14: B/W | © TVB _Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1371/image-thumb__1371__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_02.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1371/image-thumb__1371__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_02.jpg)[![Image 15: B/W | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1374/image-thumb__1374__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_11.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1374/image-thumb__1374__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_11.jpg)

**Housing and Jobs for the Resettlers**

Housing was urgently needed for the South Tyrolean resettlers in their new home. Cities and municipalities were chosen as locations that, on the one hand, were in need of workers and, on the other hand, had sufficient space available to create new housing.

Reutte offered both. Local companies such as Plansee SE, the Reuttener Textilwerke textile company, and the uniform tailoring business Karl Hoff Uniformschneiderei were in need of workers. At the same time, _Kleinfeldele_ – an open area close to the town center – was available for development.

* * *

[![Image 16: from above | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1372/image-thumb__1372__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_01.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1372/image-thumb__1372__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_01.jpg)[![Image 17: Apartment block | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1373/image-thumb__1373__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_12.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1373/image-thumb__1373__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_12.jpg)

**The Construction of the South Tyrolean Settlement in Reutte**

A total of 22 settlements were built in Tyrol. While the planning of all settlements was carried out centrally, regionally typical elements were incorporated into the architecture. Construction in Reutte began in July 1940 and was classified as essential to the war effort, which meant it was exempt from the general ban on new construction at the time. Almost exclusively local companies were commissioned for the project.

The houses were built by Alpenländische Heimstätte, a regional housing association. After two years, the first three buildings were handed over to their new residents. By November 1943, the remaining apartments, roads, and green spaces had been completed.

In total, 155 high-quality apartments were created in 18 residential buildings. For the standards of that time, the apartments were considered very comfortable and modern.

[![Image 18: summer | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1376/image-thumb__1376__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_03.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1376/image-thumb__1376__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_03.jpg)[![Image 19: View to social image | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1377/image-thumb__1377__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_04.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1377/image-thumb__1377__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_04.jpg)

**Who Lived in the Soth Tyrolean Settlement After Its Completion?**

One might assume that the settlement was inhabited exclusively by South Tyrolean resettlers. In reality, however, of the 501 people who moved in, 261 were not resettlers.

Some of the apartments were allocated to so-called “non-resettlers,” including war invalids and people affected by air raids, local residents who had made their older homes available to resettlers, as well as party officials.

* * *

**A Look Inside**

For many tenants, this was the first time they had an apartment of their own with a lockable front door. Many residents of **Reutte** were also unfamiliar with the comfort and privacy of having their own apartment, as multi-generational households were still common at the time.

An apartment for a family with one to three children was laid out as follows:

*   Bathroom – toilet with running water (instead of the pit latrines still widely used in Reutte at the time) and a washbasin; connections for a wood-fired boiler and a bathtub were provided

*   Kitchen with fitted kitchen units and a sink with running cold and hot water; a built-in cupboard beneath the window with exterior ventilation slits served as a “refrigerator”

*   Electric stove and wood-burning stove

*   Parents’ bedroom with chimney connection

*   Children’s bedroom with chimney connection

*   Cellar compartment

All other furnishings had to be provided by the residents themselves. Freight companies transported the resettlers’ few belongings to Reutte, where they were stored until the apartments were ready for occupancy.

Resettler families were often large. Extended families were either allocated apartments with two children’s bedrooms or, if required, two neighboring apartments.

In addition, the settlement included gardens for self-sufficiency, a children’s playground, a communal meeting area, and plenty of green spaces.

[![Image 20: with stove and table | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1361/image-thumb__1361__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_06.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1361/image-thumb__1361__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_06.jpg)[![Image 21: with thoughts on paper | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1362/image-thumb__1362__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_13.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1362/image-thumb__1362__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_13.jpg)

Although the South Tyrolean settlements were planned centrally, great care was taken to combine elements from the former homeland of South Tyrol with features of the new home in Reutte. One example of this is the characteristic double staircase of the Reutte Municipal Office, which can also be found in the South Tyrolean Settlement. The beautiful, large wooden balconies, on the other hand, are typical of South Tyrolean farmhouses and were likewise incorporated into the design of the settlement.

[![Image 22: Second double staircase | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1365/image-thumb__1365__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_17.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1365/image-thumb__1365__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_17.jpg)[![Image 23: with double staircase | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1360/image-thumb__1360__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_05.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1360/image-thumb__1360__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_05.jpg)

**Facade Design with a Message**

The facades of the houses feature murals created by the painter Karl Heinrich Walther Kühn, depicting scenes that reflect the ideology of the time and are well worth exploring on a walk through the settlement.

In addition to a coat-of-arms frieze at the entrance to the settlement, displaying the coats of arms of South Tyrolean towns and municipalities, the facades show scenes from rural life (with clearly defined family roles), slogans emphasizing performance and achievement, as well as ornamental rune motifs.

[![Image 24: shepherds | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1359/image-thumb__1359__areaMedia_1-5_3/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_08.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1359/image-thumb__1359__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_08.jpg)[![Image 25: Scene from peasant life | © TVB _Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1370/image-thumb__1370__areaMedia_1-5_3/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_14.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1370/image-thumb__1370__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_14.jpg)[![Image 26: entrance to the settlement | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1363/image-thumb__1363__areaMedia_1-5_3/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_16.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1363/image-thumb__1363__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_16.jpg)

**Two Murals Worth Taking a Closer Look At**

**Wolkensteiner Straße 26**

This mural features a three-part composition. The lowest level depicts a medieval knightly scene with musicians and warriors.

On the middle level, the figures shown in the center and on the left represent the last knight and the first cannoneer – Emperor Maximilian I – as well as the ship symbolizing the discovery of America.

The uppermost level portrays a family, representing life in the present at the time the mural was created.

The rooster on the far left edge of the image symbolizes morning, while the owl on the far right represents evening.

**Wolkensteiner Straße 22**

This mural refers to one of the two _Rodfuhr_ panels housed in the museum "Museum im Grünen Haus", which date back to the early 18th century. These panels depict the salt trade, which was of vital importance to the local population in the past.

[![Image 27: three-part picture | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1369/image-thumb__1369__areaMedia_1-5_3/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_07.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1369/image-thumb__1369__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_07.jpg)[![Image 28: Museum im Grünen Haus | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1375/image-thumb__1375__areaMedia_1-5_3/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_10.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1375/image-thumb__1375__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_10.jpg)[![Image 29: modified for South Tyrolians | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1368/image-thumb__1368__areaMedia_1-5_3/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_09.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1368/image-thumb__1368__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_09.jpg)

In recent years, there has been considerable debate about the preservation of the South Tyrolean Settlement. Its central location means that a much larger amount of modern living space could be created if the buildings from the 1940s were to be removed.

For now, the entire South Tyrolean Settlement remains intact and is still largely inhabited.

A total of 53% of the settlement is protected as a listed historic site and will therefore be preserved permanently. The remaining part, however, could potentially be demolished in the future.

* * *

**„Memorial Site South Tyrolean Settlement - A Planned Homeland?"**

The Museumsverein Reutte has restored an apartment at Südtirolerstraße 12 to reflect its original condition at the time of its construction. In cooperation with the Marktgemeinde Reutte, the _“Memorial Site South Tyrolean Settlement”_ was created.

The history of the South Tyrolean Settlement in Reutte is documented here in a vivid and accessible way, ensuring that it is preserved for future generations. The apartment at Südtirolerstraße 12 can be visited as part of a guided tour through the South Tyrolean Settlement.

Interest in these tours is high – school classes, travel groups, clubs, and local residents alike book guided visits and, in doing so, gain deeper insight into the more recent history of Reutte.

[![Image 30: with double staircase | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1360/image-thumb__1360__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_05.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1360/image-thumb__1360__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_05.jpg)[![Image 31](https://www.reutte.com/PDF/Grafiken/4128/image-thumb__4128__areaMedia_1-5_2/Schautafel_en.png)](https://www.reutte.com/PDF/Grafiken/4128/image-thumb__4128__lightbox/Schautafel_en.png)

**Guided Tours of the South Tyrolean Settlement Including a Visit to the Memorial Site:**

Guided tours take place on the third Wednesday of each month, on May 15 / June 19 / July 17 / August 21 / September 18 / and October 16, 2024, starting at 17:30.The meeting point is the Museum im Grünen Haus, Untermarkt 25.

The tours last approximately 1.5 hours and are free of charge with the Aktiv Card of the Reutte Nature Park Region.

# 17.05.2023 The South Tyrolean Settlement in Reutte – A Piece of History in the Heart of the Town

Today, I would like to introduce you to a part of Reutte that you may not have discovered yet, even though it is located almost right in the town center and is well worth a visit – the South Tyrolean Settlement.

**Historical Background**

After the First World War, South Tyrol was officially awarded to Italy in the Treaty of Saint-Germain in 1919. Everyday life for the South Tyrolean population – around 90% of whom were German-speaking – became increasingly difficult. German-language schools were closed, and Italians from southern regions were resettled in the area. Following Austria’s annexation by Germany in March 1938, many South Tyroleans hoped that the new ruler, Adolf Hitler, would bring South Tyrol “back home to the Reich.” These hopes were dashed when the so-called “Option” was agreed upon in the Hitler–Mussolini Agreement.

**A Forced Choice**

The “Option” forced the German-speaking South Tyrolean population to make a dramatic decision:

– They could remain in South Tyrol, renounce their cultural identity, accept Italian citizenship, and still face the risk of being resettled elsewhere within Italy

or

– They could choose German citizenship, but would then be required to leave their homeland of South Tyrol and start a new life within the German Reich.

The bitter truth for everyone involved was that, regardless of their decision, they would lose their homeland of South Tyrol.

This so-called “choice” caused a deep and lasting division within society. Entire villages and families were torn apart – those who chose to stay (“Dableiber”) could not understand those who opted to leave (“Optanten”), and vice versa.

In the vote, around 80 percent – approximately 166,000 South Tyroleans – chose the option of adopting German citizenship and emigrating. By the end of the war, about 75,000 of them had actually left. Due to the outbreak of the Second World War, the resettlement process slowed down significantly and was eventually brought to a complete halt.

[![Image 14: B/W | © TVB _Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1371/image-thumb__1371__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_02.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1371/image-thumb__1371__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_02.jpg)[![Image 15: B/W | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1374/image-thumb__1374__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_11.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1374/image-thumb__1374__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_11.jpg)

**Housing and Jobs for the Resettlers**

Housing was urgently needed for the South Tyrolean resettlers in their new home. Cities and municipalities were chosen as locations that, on the one hand, were in need of workers and, on the other hand, had sufficient space available to create new housing.

Reutte offered both. Local companies such as Plansee SE, the Reuttener Textilwerke textile company, and the uniform tailoring business Karl Hoff Uniformschneiderei were in need of workers. At the same time, _Kleinfeldele_ – an open area close to the town center – was available for development.

* * *

[![Image 16: from above | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1372/image-thumb__1372__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_01.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1372/image-thumb__1372__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_01.jpg)[![Image 17: Apartment block | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1373/image-thumb__1373__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_12.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1373/image-thumb__1373__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_12.jpg)

**The Construction of the South Tyrolean Settlement in Reutte**

A total of 22 settlements were built in Tyrol. While the planning of all settlements was carried out centrally, regionally typical elements were incorporated into the architecture. Construction in Reutte began in July 1940 and was classified as essential to the war effort, which meant it was exempt from the general ban on new construction at the time. Almost exclusively local companies were commissioned for the project.

The houses were built by Alpenländische Heimstätte, a regional housing association. After two years, the first three buildings were handed over to their new residents. By November 1943, the remaining apartments, roads, and green spaces had been completed.

In total, 155 high-quality apartments were created in 18 residential buildings. For the standards of that time, the apartments were considered very comfortable and modern.

[![Image 18: summer | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1376/image-thumb__1376__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_03.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1376/image-thumb__1376__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_03.jpg)[![Image 19: View to social image | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1377/image-thumb__1377__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_04.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1377/image-thumb__1377__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_04.jpg)

**Who Lived in the Soth Tyrolean Settlement After Its Completion?**

One might assume that the settlement was inhabited exclusively by South Tyrolean resettlers. In reality, however, of the 501 people who moved in, 261 were not resettlers.

Some of the apartments were allocated to so-called “non-resettlers,” including war invalids and people affected by air raids, local residents who had made their older homes available to resettlers, as well as party officials.

* * *

**A Look Inside**

For many tenants, this was the first time they had an apartment of their own with a lockable front door. Many residents of **Reutte** were also unfamiliar with the comfort and privacy of having their own apartment, as multi-generational households were still common at the time.

An apartment for a family with one to three children was laid out as follows:

*   Bathroom – toilet with running water (instead of the pit latrines still widely used in Reutte at the time) and a washbasin; connections for a wood-fired boiler and a bathtub were provided

*   Kitchen with fitted kitchen units and a sink with running cold and hot water; a built-in cupboard beneath the window with exterior ventilation slits served as a “refrigerator”

*   Electric stove and wood-burning stove

*   Parents’ bedroom with chimney connection

*   Children’s bedroom with chimney connection

*   Cellar compartment

All other furnishings had to be provided by the residents themselves. Freight companies transported the resettlers’ few belongings to Reutte, where they were stored until the apartments were ready for occupancy.

Resettler families were often large. Extended families were either allocated apartments with two children’s bedrooms or, if required, two neighboring apartments.

In addition, the settlement included gardens for self-sufficiency, a children’s playground, a communal meeting area, and plenty of green spaces.

[![Image 20: with stove and table | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1361/image-thumb__1361__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_06.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1361/image-thumb__1361__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_06.jpg)[![Image 21: with thoughts on paper | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1362/image-thumb__1362__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_13.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1362/image-thumb__1362__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_13.jpg)

Although the South Tyrolean settlements were planned centrally, great care was taken to combine elements from the former homeland of South Tyrol with features of the new home in Reutte. One example of this is the characteristic double staircase of the Reutte Municipal Office, which can also be found in the South Tyrolean Settlement. The beautiful, large wooden balconies, on the other hand, are typical of South Tyrolean farmhouses and were likewise incorporated into the design of the settlement.

[![Image 22: Second double staircase | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1365/image-thumb__1365__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_17.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1365/image-thumb__1365__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_17.jpg)[![Image 23: with double staircase | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1360/image-thumb__1360__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_05.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1360/image-thumb__1360__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_05.jpg)

**Facade Design with a Message**

The facades of the houses feature murals created by the painter Karl Heinrich Walther Kühn, depicting scenes that reflect the ideology of the time and are well worth exploring on a walk through the settlement.

In addition to a coat-of-arms frieze at the entrance to the settlement, displaying the coats of arms of South Tyrolean towns and municipalities, the facades show scenes from rural life (with clearly defined family roles), slogans emphasizing performance and achievement, as well as ornamental rune motifs.

[![Image 24: shepherds | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1359/image-thumb__1359__areaMedia_1-5_3/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_08.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1359/image-thumb__1359__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_08.jpg)[![Image 25: Scene from peasant life | © TVB _Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1370/image-thumb__1370__areaMedia_1-5_3/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_14.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1370/image-thumb__1370__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_14.jpg)[![Image 26: entrance to the settlement | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1363/image-thumb__1363__areaMedia_1-5_3/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_16.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1363/image-thumb__1363__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_16.jpg)

**Two Murals Worth Taking a Closer Look At**

**Wolkensteiner Straße 26**

This mural features a three-part composition. The lowest level depicts a medieval knightly scene with musicians and warriors.

On the middle level, the figures shown in the center and on the left represent the last knight and the first cannoneer – Emperor Maximilian I – as well as the ship symbolizing the discovery of America.

The uppermost level portrays a family, representing life in the present at the time the mural was created.

The rooster on the far left edge of the image symbolizes morning, while the owl on the far right represents evening.

**Wolkensteiner Straße 22**

This mural refers to one of the two _Rodfuhr_ panels housed in the museum "Museum im Grünen Haus", which date back to the early 18th century. These panels depict the salt trade, which was of vital importance to the local population in the past.

[![Image 27: three-part picture | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1369/image-thumb__1369__areaMedia_1-5_3/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_07.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1369/image-thumb__1369__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_07.jpg)[![Image 28: Museum im Grünen Haus | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1375/image-thumb__1375__areaMedia_1-5_3/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_10.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1375/image-thumb__1375__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_10.jpg)[![Image 29: modified for South Tyrolians | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1368/image-thumb__1368__areaMedia_1-5_3/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_09.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1368/image-thumb__1368__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_09.jpg)

In recent years, there has been considerable debate about the preservation of the South Tyrolean Settlement. Its central location means that a much larger amount of modern living space could be created if the buildings from the 1940s were to be removed.

For now, the entire South Tyrolean Settlement remains intact and is still largely inhabited.

A total of 53% of the settlement is protected as a listed historic site and will therefore be preserved permanently. The remaining part, however, could potentially be demolished in the future.

* * *

**„Memorial Site South Tyrolean Settlement - A Planned Homeland?"**

The Museumsverein Reutte has restored an apartment at Südtirolerstraße 12 to reflect its original condition at the time of its construction. In cooperation with the Marktgemeinde Reutte, the _“Memorial Site South Tyrolean Settlement”_ was created.

The history of the South Tyrolean Settlement in Reutte is documented here in a vivid and accessible way, ensuring that it is preserved for future generations. The apartment at Südtirolerstraße 12 can be visited as part of a guided tour through the South Tyrolean Settlement.

Interest in these tours is high – school classes, travel groups, clubs, and local residents alike book guided visits and, in doing so, gain deeper insight into the more recent history of Reutte.

[![Image 30: with double staircase | © TVB Naturparkregion Reutte](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1360/image-thumb__1360__areaMedia_1-5_2/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_05.jpg)](https://www.reutte.com/Bilder/NaturparkregionReutte/Blog/SuedtirolerSiedlung/1360/image-thumb__1360__lightbox/Blog-SuedtirolerSiedlung_TVBNaturparkregionReutte_05.jpg)[![Image 31](https://www.reutte.com/PDF/Grafiken/4128/image-thumb__4128__areaMedia_1-5_2/Schautafel_en.png)](https://www.reutte.com/PDF/Grafiken/4128/image-thumb__4128__lightbox/Schautafel_en.png)

**Guided Tours of the South Tyrolean Settlement Including a Visit to the Memorial Site:**

Guided tours take place on the third Wednesday of each month, on May 15 / June 19 / July 17 / August 21 / September 18 / and October 16, 2024, starting at 17:30.The meeting point is the Museum im Grünen Haus, Untermarkt 25.

The tours last approximately 1.5 hours and are free of charge with the Aktiv Card of the Reutte Nature Park Region.

“For once you have tasted flight you will walk the earth with your
eyes turned skywards, for there you have been and there you will long
to return.” – Leonardo da Vinci

Ever since man took to the skies - when that first Wright Brothers 59-second flight
on December 17, 1903 sailed above the Kitty Hawk dunes - pilots have been pushing
their flying machines in pursuit of greatness. Tests of skill, endurance, and agility have
taken fearless pilots across countries, over oceans, and to the ver y reaches of space.
The 53-year aerial tradition known as the “Hayward Air Rally” will be lifting off
Thursday, June 22 – Sunday, June 25 from the Hayward Executive Airport to
Reno/Stead, Nevada, via Redding, California, equaling approximately 250 to
300 nautical miles per leg. It is the longest running continuous air rally of its kind in
the countr y. Between 25 to 35 general aviation flight crews will soar above the clouds
in a race that is not judged on speed or who makes it to the finish line first. In fact,

June 6, 2017
An Open Letter to the Fremont Community:

As Mayor of the City of Fremont, and on behalf of the entire City Council, I’d like to take this opportunity to reaffirm the
City’s commitment to the fight against climate change. We understand that the threats of global warming are real and thus we
remain steadfast in our ambitious goals of reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and achieving community-wide sustainability.
Fremont will continue to demonstrate strong leadership in these efforts.
Fremont’s commitment to climate action planning and implementation dates back to 2006 when the City signed onto the
U.S. Conference of Mayors Climate Protection Agreement to meet or exceed the Kyoto Protocol goals of reducing human-emitted
greenhouse gases. In 2011, the City’s award-winning General Plan put forth the vision for Fremont  to ser ve as a national model of
how an auto-oriented suburb can evolve into a sustainable, strategically urban, modern city. By 2012, Council adopted the
City’s first Climate Action Plan, setting a goal to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 25 percent from a 2005 baseline by the
year 2020 and providing a roadmap for these reductions. In December 2015, Fremont was a signator y to the Compact of Mayors,
an agreement by cities around the world to reduce GHG emissions and enhance resilience; the Compact of Mayors is now known
as the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate & Energy.
Some notable examples of Fremont’s leadership in this area include:
  Solar Friendly Initiatives  such as the reduction in solar permitting fees, over-the-counter solar plan review, discounted solar
purchasing through the Bay Area SunShares program, and most recently the adoption of a mandator y solar ordinance for new
residential construction.
  Solar projects  at City facilities including the installation of solar carports at the Police Building Complex, Aqua Adventure
Waterpark, Ir vington Community Center, and Maintenance Center.
  Zero emissions vehicle  readiness planning, including the installation of publicly accessible electric vehicle charging
stations and requirements for the installation of electric vehicle charging infrastructure in new single-family, multifamily, and
non-residential developments.
  Support and encouragement of waste reduction  efforts through education, incentives, and technical assistance for recycling
and food waste capture in the residential and business sectors.
  Creation of a Sustainability Commission  to advise the Council on emerging policy issues related to environmental
sustainability.
  Implementation of a comprehensive energy and water savings  project to upgrade all City-owned streetlights, park lights,
and facility lights to the most efficient LED technologies, as well as to upgrade the efficiency of City plumbing fixtures and
irrigation systems.
Sustainability is not only a strong value in this community but also an important driver of our economy. With over 50 cleantech
companies in Fremont, we as a City are supporting innovation across the entire smart grid value chain. Fremont is a recognized
pioneer in the cleantech economy, with our semiconductor roots paving the way for today’s advances in ever ything from LEDs and
energy storage to solar and electric vehicles. As an example of our long-term commitment, for nearly a decade, we have offered a
business tax exemption for cleantech companies, as a gesture of our partnership in their growth. And the City maintains strong ties
to industr y associations, such as the Cleantech Open, California Clean Energy Fund, and GreenBiz, to champion the causes of
cleantech industries in our region and beyond.
To further signal Fremont’s dedication to continue efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and alleviate the impacts of global
warming, I recently signed onto a coalition statement to the domestic and international community that speaks to the urgency of
staving off climate change and shows our continued support for the Paris Climate Accord. You can find the full statement online at
www.WeAreStillIn.com, which includes a growing list of city leaders, governors, universities, and businesses as its signatories.
Additionally, I signed the “Mayor’s for 100% Clean Energy,” an initiative of the Sierra Club’s Ready for 100 Campaign and
viewable at www.sierraclub.org/ready-for-100/mayors-for-clean-energy, and the “ We are Climate Mayors,” which is an
initiative of the Mayors’ National Climate Action Agenda (MNCAA) and viewable at https://medium.com/@ClimateMayors/cli-
mate-mayors-commit-to-adopt-honor-and-uphold-paris-climate-agreement-goals-ba566e260097.
How Can You Help?
Finally, understanding that ever yone can make choices that will greatly reduce our global warming impacts, I invite the
entire community (residents, businesses, and schools) to join us in taking steps to stop global warming. By reducing excessive
consumption, using clean and renewable energy resources, buying locally produced products, and recycling, reusing, and
composting our waste, we will continue to pave the way for a more vibrant and healthier future, sustaining the planet for
generations to come. Join the Fremont Green Challenge and help create a clean, vibrant, and healthy future for our families.
Visit this local climate action engagement platform at www.FremontGreenChallenge.org to learn more.
For more information about the City of Fremont’s environmental sustainability efforts go to www.Fremont.gov/Sustainability.
Sincerely,

Lily Mei

300 nautical miles per leg. It is the longest running continuous air rally of its kind in

flights are judged on the pilot’s abilities to navigate using VFR (visual flight rules).
